steps: Step 1, Read a bar graph: bars show pupils per sport. Football 12, cricket 9, tennis 5, swimming 9. The scale is 1 per square, so read the top of each bar against the axis.
Step 2, Find the mode: the value that occurs most often. In 12, 9, 5, 9 the number 9 appears twice, so the mode is 9. In the graph, cricket and swimming share it.
Step 3, Line graph: temperatures at 6, 8, 10, 12 o'clock were 18, 21, 26, 29 degrees. The line rises each time. From 8 to 10 the rise is 26 - 21 = 5 degrees.
Step 4, Find the greatest rise: between 6 and 8 the rise is 3, 8 to 10 is 5, 10 to 12 is 3. The steepest part of the line is 8 to 10, with a rise of 5.
Step 5, Total and difference from bars: total pupils = 12 + 9 + 5 + 9 = 35. Football minus tennis is 12 - 5 = 7. State what the numbers mean in a sentence.
Step 6, Your turn: find the mode of 4, 7, 7, 3, 7, 4 and the rise from 21 to 29 degrees. Answer: mode is 7, which appears three times; rise is 8 degrees.

Step 1, Show that air expands when heated. Put a balloon over the mouth of a bottle and place the bottle in a warm water bath at 60 C. The balloon inflates as the air expands and becomes less dense, which is why warm air rises.

Step 2, Explain wind. Land near a coast heats faster in daytime. Warm air over land rises, creating low pressure. Cooler air from the sea, at higher pressure, flows in as a sea breeze. At night it reverses.

Step 3, Show air pressure. A glass full of water covered with card and inverted holds the card because air pressure pushing up on the card is larger than the weight of the water. Air presses on everything.

Step 4, Describe a cyclone. Warm ocean water, above about 26.5 C, evaporates and the rising moist air makes a low-pressure centre. Winds spiral inward at over 120 km per hour. The calm centre is the eye, with heavy clouds in the eyewall.
Step 5, Cyclone safety: listen to weather warnings, keep a torch, radio, dry food and drinking water, stay indoors away from windows, and move to a shelter if told to. Do not go near the sea.
Step 6, Your turn: air at one place is at 1000 hPa and at another is 1010 hPa. Which way does the wind blow? Answer: from the 1010 hPa place toward the 1000 hPa low-pressure place.

Step 1, Count from one to ten: un, deux, trois, quatre, cinq, six, sept, huit, neuf, dix. Say them with your fingers. The final x of deux is silent, but the x of dix sounds like s, and the t of huit is pronounced. Repeat three times, getting faster.

Step 2, Learn colours: rouge [red], bleu [blue], jaune [yellow], vert [green], noir [black], blanc [white]. Hold up coloured objects and ask: C'est de quelle couleur ? [What colour is it?] Answer: C'est rouge. [It is red.]

Step 3, Put numbers and things together. J'ai trois crayons. [I have three pencils.] J'ai deux balles rouges. [I have two red balls.] Combien de pommes ? [How many apples?] Cinq pommes. [Five apples.] Practise with real objects on your desk.

Step 4, Dialogue with a friend. Tom : Quelle est ta couleur préférée ? [What is your favourite colour?] Sara : Ma couleur préférée est le bleu. [My favourite colour is blue.] Tom : Moi, j'aime le vert. [I like green.] Sara : Super ! [Great!]

Step 5, Fix an error. A child says un balle. Correction: une balle, because balle is feminine. Say un crayon but une gomme. With colours, many add an e for feminine: une pomme verte [a green apple], une chaise blanche [a white chair].

Step 6, Your turn: say you have four yellow pencils and one blue ball. Model answer: J'ai quatre crayons jaunes et une balle bleue. [I have four yellow pencils and a blue ball.] Then ask a friend: Combien de crayons ? [How many pencils?]

Step 1, Say the first vowels: अ आ इ ई उ ऊ ए ऐ ओ औ. Say each sound slowly: a, aa, i, ee, u, oo, e, ai, o, au. Trace each letter in the air with your finger, and draw the top line (shirorekha) last, after the letter is written.
Step 2, Link vowels to words. अ से अनार [A for pomegranate], आ से आम [Aa for mango], इ से इमली [I for tamarind], उ से उल्लू [U for owl]. Say the full line each time, like a chant: अ से अनार।

Step 3, Say the first consonants: क ख ग घ. क से कमल [K for lotus], ख से खरगोश [Kh for rabbit], ग से गमला [G for flower pot], घ से घर [Gh for house]. Notice that each consonant carries a short a sound.

Step 4, Write with a headline. Every letter in क, ख, ग, घ hangs from a line drawn on top, called शिरोरेखा [the headline]. Write each letter three times: क क क, ख ख ख. Then read your line aloud: कमल, खरगोश, घर.

Step 5, Fix an error. A learner writes the letters of कमल without the top line and reads क as k with no vowel. Correction: draw the line on top of every letter, and say each consonant with its short a: ka-ma-la, then read the whole word as कमल [lotus].
Step 6, Your turn: say and write च छ ज with one word each. Model answer: च से चम्मच [spoon], छ से छाता [umbrella], ज से जहाज़ [ship]. Write each letter three times with its headline.

Step 1, Start with a base word and a prefix. un- means not: happy becomes unhappy. re- means again: write becomes rewrite. dis- means not or opposite: agree becomes disagree. Reason: a prefix goes at the front and changes the meaning.

Step 2, Build with suffixes. -ful means full of: care becomes careful. -less means without: care becomes careless. -ly turns an adjective into an adverb: slow becomes slowly. Reason: a suffix goes at the end.
Step 3, Work out meanings by parts. "Unforgettable" = un- (not) + forget + -able (can be). Meaning: not able to be forgotten. Reason: splitting a word into parts reveals its meaning.

Step 4, Apply spelling rules. Drop silent e before -ing and -able: "hope" becomes "hoping". Change y to i before a suffix: "happy" becomes "happiness". Double the consonant in "run" before -ing: "running".
Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "unhapyness". Right: "unhappiness" (un + happy, y to i, + ness). Another error: "carefull". Right: "careful" (the suffix is -ful with one l).

Step 6, Use new words in context. "The boy was careless and left his bag. His teacher was disappointed. He promised to recheck his work." Underline the prefix or suffix in each: careless, disappointed, recheck.

Step 7, Your turn. Build and define three words using un-, re- and -ful. Model answer: "unlock" (undo a lock); "retell" (tell again); "helpful" (full of help). Use one in a sentence: "She was helpful."
Step 1, Plan the talk in four short parts: greeting, name and age, family, likes. Reason: four small parts are easy to remember and give the talk a clear order.

Step 2, Write the model talk. "Hello. My name is Ali. I am eight. I have a mother, a father and one sister. I like football and rice." That is a greeting and four short sentences. Each sentence has a subject and a verb.
Step 3, Practise saying each sentence aloud slowly. Stress the key words: "My name is ALI." "I am EIGHT." Reason: clear stress and a steady pace matter more than speed.
Step 4, Add one extra detail with "and". Model: "I have a cat and a dog." Reason: "and" joins two things in one sentence, so your talk sounds smoother.
Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "I am have a sister." Right: "I have a sister." We use "am" or "have", not both. Another error: "My name Ali." Right: "My name is Ali."

Step 6, Finish with a polite ending and a question. Model: "Thank you. Do you have any questions?" Answer a question like "How old are you?" with "I am eight." Reason: a closing line tells the listener the talk is over.
Step 7, Your turn. Write your own six-line talk. Model answer: "Hello. My name is Maya. I am nine. I have a brother and a cat. I like apples. Thank you."

Step 1, Sit and set up: Amina sits with both feet on the floor, the screen at eye level, and one hand on the mouse. She finds the pointer arrow on the screen and moves the mouse slowly until the arrow touches the big green square.

Step 2, Click: With the arrow on the green square, Amina presses the left button once and lets go. The square turns yellow. One quick press is a click. She says 'click' aloud each time to remember the single press.

Step 3, Drag: Amina puts the arrow on a red ball, holds the left button down, slides the mouse to the basket on the right, then lets go. The ball drops into the basket. Hold, move, release is called dragging.

Step 4, Find letters: Her teacher shows a box and the letters A, M, I, N. Amina looks at the keyboard, finds the A key on the left side of the middle row, and presses it once. An 'a' appears in the box.
Step 5, Type the name: She holds the Shift key with her little finger while pressing A to make a capital, so the first letter is right. Next come m, i, n, a. The screen shows Amina, five letters.

Step 6, Check and fix: She reads the screen letter by letter, touching each one with the pointer: A-m-i-n-a. All five match. If a letter were wrong she would press Backspace once to remove the last letter and type again.

Your turn: Your name is Omar. Click the blue button, drag a star into a box, then type your name with a capital O. Model answer: O comes from Shift plus the O key, then m, a, r. The screen shows Omar, four letters, and the star sits inside the box.

Step 1, The raw data: Raed's sheet has 7 rows: Ali 72; bana 91; Cyrus blank; Dina 88; Dina 88; Eman 65; Fadi 150. The maximum score is 100, so some entries look wrong. Before analysis the data must be cleaned.

Step 2, Fix format: He makes names consistent by changing bana to Bana and trimming extra spaces. Consistent text means sorting and searching work properly. Hidden extra spaces or odd capitals can make the same name look different to a computer.
Step 3, Remove duplicates: Dina 88 appears twice, so he deletes one copy. The sheet now has 6 rows. Duplicates would count one student twice and distort totals and averages.

Step 4, Handle missing and impossible values: Cyrus has no score, so he marks it as missing and leaves it out. Fadi 150 is above 100, so he flags it as an error to check with the teacher. Valid rows left: Ali, Bana, Dina, Eman.
Step 5, Sort and summarise: Sorting scores highest first gives Bana 91, Dina 88, Ali 72, Eman 65. The maximum is 91 and the minimum is 65. The sum is 72 plus 91 plus 88 plus 65, which is 316.

Step 6, Average and record: The average is 316 divided by 4, which is 79. He writes a note: 4 valid of 7 original rows; 1 duplicate, 1 missing and 1 impossible. Recording what was removed keeps the analysis honest.
Your turn: Scores 60, 80, blank, 80 (duplicate student), 120. Clean and average. Model answer: remove the duplicate 80, ignore blank, flag 120, leaving 60 and 80; the average is 70.
Step 1, The project: Aref leads a team of four on a lab project measuring the time a trolley takes to roll down a ramp. Roles: Aref leads, Dina measures, Hamad records, Sara analyses the data.

Step 2, Ethical rules: Record every trial honestly, do not change data to match a hoped result, give credit for help and report all methods. These rules are agreed and written in the project log before the first trial.
Step 3, The data: Five timing trials in seconds are 12.1, 12.3, 11.9, 12.2 and 14.8. The sum is 63.3, so the mean is 63.3 divided by 5, which is 12.66 seconds. The last result is far from the others.

Step 4, The temptation: Hamad suggests deleting 14.8 without saying so, because it spoils the neat result. Aref asks, 'Would we be comfortable explaining this to our teacher?' The team decides the outlier cannot be silently removed.

Step 5, The honest treatment: They investigate and find that Dina stopped the timer late on trial 5. They report all five values and explain the probable error. Without that trial the mean is 48.5 divided by 4, which is 12.125 seconds.

Step 6, Review the leadership: The report shows both means, 12.66 and 12.125, and states the reason. The team rates itself out of 5: honesty 5, method 4, teamwork 4. Aref notes that one more trial would have helped. Honest reporting makes results trustworthy.

Your turn: Trials 8.0, 8.2, 8.1 and 9.9. What do you report? Model answer: all four values; mean with all is 34.2 divided by 4, which is 8.55; without 9.9 it is 8.1; explain the cause and repeat the trial.
